title_tag: Vegan Eye Cream Review: A Crunchy Mom's Honest Take (2026)
meta_desc: I switched my eye cream after my third baby. Here's why I picked Leaf & Bird's vegan peptide eye gel-cream — and what 60 days actually looked like.
image_alt: Vegan peptide eye cream jar on linen — Leaf & Bird vegan eye cream review

mainEntity.name: Is this eye cream actually vegan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The Peptide Eye Gel-Cream is fully vegan — no beeswax, no lanolin, no animal-derived collagen or peptides. The Acetyl Tetrapeptide-5 in it is a synthetic peptide, not animal-sourced.

mainEntity.name: Can I use it during pregnancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: I'm not your doctor, so this isn't medical advice — run any product past your OB. That said, the formula was built without retinoids, salicylic acid, or hydroquinone, which are the actives most pregnancy guidance flags. I have a separate post on which eye cream ingredients I'd avoid in pregnancy and why.

mainEntity.name: How is it different from a caffeine eye cream?

acceptedAnswer.text: Caffeine eye creams constrict blood vessels for a short-term de-puffing look but don't really do anything for skin texture or fine lines long-term. This skips caffeine entirely and uses peptides, niacinamide, and squalane — aimed at hydration and supporting skin over time, not temporary cosmetic effects.

mainEntity.name: Will it make a noticeable difference in two weeks?

acceptedAnswer.text: Honestly, no — and I'd be skeptical of any eye cream that promises that. In my use, the first thing I noticed in week one was the absence of irritation. Visible-difference stuff started around day thirty and felt more settled at day sixty.

mainEntity.name: What's the active ingredient doing the work?

acceptedAnswer.text: The headlining peptide is Acetyl Tetrapeptide-5, with a research base behind it for the under-eye area. The formula also uses niacinamide for tone and squalane for hydration. No retinol, no caffeine, no fragrance.

mainEntity.name: Is $30.99 a fair price for an eye cream?

acceptedAnswer.text: I think so, and I built it that way on purpose. A drugstore eye cream might run $15 but be mostly water and dimethicone. A department-store one with a similar peptide profile usually starts at $60–$80. $30.99 covers real actives in a clean formula without paying for marketing or packaging.
